plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), comparing the orientations of polar HF molecules in the absence and presence of an external electric field. In panel (a), six HF molecules — each depicted as a large green fluorine sphere carrying a δ− partial charge bonded to a smaller white hydrogen sphere carrying a δ+ partial charge — are shown between two uncharged gray plates in random, disordered orientations, reflecting the thermally averaged state when no aligning force is present. In panel (b), an electric field is applied between a negatively charged left plate (labeled −) and a positively charged right plate (labeled +), and five HF molecules are now all uniformly aligned with the δ+ hydrogen end directed toward the negative plate and the δ− fluorine end directed toward the positive plate, demonstrating that the dipole responds to the field direction. This figure illustrates the physical mechanism by which polar molecules align in an electric field and provides the molecular-level basis for understanding how polarity governs intermolecular interactions and the "like dissolves like" principle in solvent chemistry.

demo_steps.title: No electric field
demo_steps.narration: The HCl molecules are randomly oriented between neutral gray plates. Their δ+ and δ− ends are fixed on each molecule, but the molecular dipoles point in different directions overall.

demo_steps.title: Weak applied field
demo_steps.narration: Turning on a weak field introduces a preferred direction. Most molecules rotate partway so the white δ+ hydrogen end tends toward the negative plate, but the alignment remains imperfect.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a single switchable panel rather than displaying panels (a) and (b) side by side. World coordinates: +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, +Z is the oblique receding direction. Overall active panel spans about X = −3.4 to +3.4 and Y = −3.2 to +3.2. Plates: left plate centered at x = −3.1, right plate centered at x = +3.1; each is a tall slab about 0.18 × 6.2 × 0.55 world units, with the narrow oblique side face receding slightly up/right in screen space. No-field view: white background between plates, no plate charge signs. Applied-field view: pale cream field rectangle #fff4d0 from x = −2.9 to +2.9 and y = −3.0 to +3.0, bounded by the two plates. Plates are light gray #c7c9cc with darker side faces #9a9a9a and black outlines. Molecules: large chlorine sphere radius about 0.42, green #6fbd3f with lighter highlight #bce98a; small hydrogen sphere radius about 0.28, white #f8f8f8 with light gray shadow. Center-to-center H–Cl distance about 0.52 so the spheres overlap like the source. In no-field panel (a), use five molecule centers and random dipole directions matching the source: center-left at (−1.75, +0.95) with H upper-left and Cl lower-right; lower-left at (−1.9, −2.0) with H lower-right and Cl upper-left; upper-right at (+1.0, +2.35) with H upper-right and Cl lower-left; central at (+0.45, +0.35) with H downward and Cl upward; lower-right at (+1.05, −1.65) with H right/up and Cl left/down. In applied-field panel (b), use five molecule centers matching the source layout: upper-right at (+1.55, +2.35), mid-left at (−1.35, +0.85), lower-left at (−1.45, −0.55), lower-right at (+1.55, −1.55), bottom-left at (−1.35, −2.65). All applied-field molecules point horizontally with H on the left and Cl on the right: molecular axis angle 0 degrees from left-to-right H→Cl, so δ+ is on the left side and δ− on the right side. The negative plate label '−' sits near x = −2.95, y = +2.9; the positive plate label '+' sits near x = +2.95, y = +2.9. The 'Electric field' label is near x = −0.5, y = +3.25 with a short black slanted line from about (−0.35, +2.95) to (−0.65, +3.55), visually matching the source. Panel label '(a)' or '(b)' appears centered below the panel at y = −3.45. Field strength maps to angular interpolation: strength 0 keeps the no-field random angles; strength 1 sets every molecule to the applied-field horizontal alignment; intermediate values rotate each molecule toward horizontal with a small residual random angular offset of roughly ±30 degrees at strength 0.35.
interactionPlan.notes: Render spheres with MeshPhongMaterial or MeshStandardMaterial and a strong upper-left key light to reproduce the glossy textbook highlights. Keep the camera/front projection fixed; do not add orbit controls because the educational point is orientation relative to plates, not hidden 3D structure. Implement the toggle by crossfading the background, plate charge labels, electric-field label, and molecule target positions/orientations. The alignment animation should start from the current random no-field orientations and ease the molecule rotations into the orientation specified by fieldStrength; use about 1.5 seconds with cubic ease-out. Attach δ+ and δ− labels to the hydrogen and chlorine ends so labels move and rotate consistently during the animation.

authoredContext:
Polar molecules tend to align when placed in an electric field with the positive end of the molecule oriented toward the negative plate and the negative end toward the positive plate ( ). We can use an electrically charged object to attract polar molecules, but nonpolar molecules are not attracted. Also, polar solvents are better at dissolving polar substances, and nonpolar solvents are better at dissolving nonpolar substances.

Polarity Simulations Open the molecule polarity simulation and select the “Three Atoms” tab at the top. This should display a molecule ABC with three electronegativity adjustors. You can display or hide the bond moments, molecular dipoles, and partial charges at the right. Turning on the Electric Field will show whether the molecule moves when exposed to a field, similar to .

(a) Molecules are always randomly distributed in the liquid state in the absence of an electric field. (b) When an electric field is applied, polar molecules like HF will align to the dipoles with the field direction.

Two diagrams are shown and labeled “a” and “b.” Diagram a shows two vertical, gray electrodes. There are five molecules in between. The molecules are separate from one another and are composed of a hydrogen atom bonded to a fluorine atom. The fluorine atom is labeled with a dipole symbol and a superscripted negative sign while the hydrogen atom is labeled with a dipole symbol and a superscripted positive sign. The molecules are randomly oriented in the space. The right diagram also shows two vertical gray electrodes, the left labeled as negative and the right labeled as positive. The space between is yellow. The same molecules are present, but this time they are all facing horizontally, with the hydrogen-end of each molecule facing toward the negative electrode.

discrepancies: The original shows panels (a) and (b) side by side, while the generated figure shows only one panel at a time behind a toggle, reducing the immediate comparison between random and aligned orientations.
The generated molecules are darker, glossier 3D ball models than the lighter green/white shaded textbook-style molecules in the source.
The capacitor plates are rendered as thick rectangular 3D slabs rather than the thin skewed gray plates with simple gradient shading in the source.
When the field is on, the generated figure adds blue-gray rotational arc paths that are not present in the source figure.
Panel (b) is controlled by a continuous field-strength slider and weak-field intermediate state, whereas the source only depicts the off/random and on/aligned cases.
evaluation.notes: The figure captures the main HCl dipole alignment concept well with useful controls, but it differs from the textbook layout and adds extra interaction/arc elements not shown in the source.
action_items: Provide a side-by-side view of panels (a) and (b), or add a clear split-screen mode matching the original figure.
Lighten the green chlorine spheres and reduce excessive glossy contrast to better match the source styling.
Make the plates thinner and more like the skewed gray plates in the textbook figure.
Hide the rotational arc paths by default in the source-matching panel view.

feedback.rationale: The concept is accurate, but the issues are concrete generation-level fidelity problems such as side-by-side layout, styling, plate geometry, and hiding hallucinated arc/slider elements.
